items.title: Why do politicians often want to change the school curriculum?
items.summary: Both sides of Australian politics are saying the school curriculum needs to change.

items.title: Quantum device simulates matter popping into existence
items.summary: A research team led by faculty at the Duke Quantum Center (DQC) has observed string-breaking dynamics related to particle-antiparticle formation on a quantum simulator, among the first such observations in quantum physics.

items.title: Could negative mass exist and be observed?
items.summary: Unlike electric charge, as far as we know all mass is positive, and positive masses attract one another. Could negative mass exist, and if so, what would be the ramifications?

items.title: Arts and culture key to inclusive climate action
items.summary: The arts, cultural and creative sectors can act as powerful catalysts for climate action, changing how people understand, engage with and act on climate change, new research from University College Cork (UCC) has found.

items.summary: A major Swedish study of 3.7 million people has found that rare TORCH infections passed from a pregnant woman to the fetus are linked to much higher risks of autism and intellectual disability later in life. items.summary: Tiny plantlike organisms called phytoplankton that form the base of marine food webs topped by orcas, whales and sharks usually get eaten or slowly sink to the seafloor, carrying carbon as they go. items.summary: A new decision-making tool developed by Queensland University of Technology researchers could help governments, businesses and organizations make more reliable decisions for such projects as major infrastructure and public policy development. items.title: Breakthrough drug reverses skin aging and dramatically speeds healing
items.summary: A topical drug that removes aging, damaged cells helped older mice heal skin wounds significantly faster. The treatment appeared to reactivate repair pathways involved in inflammation, collagen production, and new blood vessel growth.

items.title: When everyday sounds trigger big feelings: Inside misophonia research
items.summary: Misophonia causes strong emotions in response to everyday sounds like chewing or sniffing. The condition often involves feelings of immediate distress or anger. This can be confusing and upsetting for children, adults and their families or friends.

items.title: Canadian musicians facing multi-front squeeze from AI, streaming and venue closures
items.summary: New research shows Canadian musicians are feeling increasingly hostile toward the tech industry and advances like generative AI, which they say are devaluing art and making it harder to gain listeners and earn money from music.

items.title: Blood test falls short in quest to detect gastric ulcer pain in horses
items.summary: A new study led by Australian veterinarians has exposed the challenge of identifying pain in horses with gastric ulcers and highlights an urgent need to better detect when horses are suffering.

items.title: The Arctic sea ice melt season grew longer for decades, but something strange happened around 2010
items.summary: The Arctic sea ice melt season is roughly 40 days longer than it was in 1979, yet its rapid expansion unexpectedly leveled off around 2010. items.title: First stellar stream beyond the Milky Way could reveal dark matter
items.summary: Astronomers have discovered the first globular cluster stellar stream beyond the Milky Way, opening a new way to study dark matter in distant galaxies. These faint trails of stars trace a galaxy’s gravitational structure and could eventually help scientists map invisible matter across the universe.

items.summary: There's more to growing a plant than just adding enough water and providing adequate sunlight.

items.summary: Over 1 million plastic water bottles are bought globally every minute. That translates into more than 1.3 billion every day and more than 500 billion every year. items.summary: Scandinavian museums are trying to move beyond the familiar image of Vikings as sword-wielding male warriors, highlighting women, farmers, traders, and a far more complicated society. items.summary: Stonehenge’s six-ton Altar Stone may have been carried from Scotland to Dogger Bank by glaciers before prehistoric people transported it hundreds of kilometers to Salisbury Plain. items.summary: A pigeon turning its head might seem an unlikely electricity generator. items.title: Typhoon Dujuan leaves seven dead in Japan from landslides, flooding
items.summary: Typhoon Dujuan left seven people dead and five others missing Tuesday after the storm triggered landslides and flooding in the greater Tokyo area, Kyodo News reported, citing authorities.

items.title: UK to launch new military space squadron to protect satellites
items.summary: Britain announced Wednesday that it will launch a new military space squadron to defend the country's satellites, the latest move as countries race to develop military space capabilities.
